# NIST AI 100-2e2025 — Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations

> **External, not NASA governance.** Useful for comparison and vocabulary. It never establishes
> what NASA requires, and must not be cited as NASA coverage.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / owner** | National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), with Northeastern University, Cisco, and the U.K. AI Security Institute as co-authoring institutions |
| **Kind** | research (taxonomy and terminology report) |
| **Status** | NIST AI 100-2e2025, "Approved by the NIST Editorial Review Board on 2025-03-20" [p.3]; final; "e2025" marks this as the 2025 edition, superseding an earlier NIST AI 100-2 edition (paraphrase; original-edition date not itself verified) |
| **Where to get it** | free public download, DOI https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025; also at https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ai/100/2/e2025/final; publication number NIST AI 100-2e2025 |
| **Binds whom** | no one (voluntary) — it is a terminology/taxonomy report, not a framework or mandate; it names no compliance obligation |

**What it is good for, relative to NASA's documents.** It is the detailed vocabulary for adversarial
machine learning that NASA's documents do not themselves define — attack classes, attacker goals,
and named mitigations for both predictive AI (Sec. 2) and generative AI (Sec. 3) (our reading). Where
a risk candidate concerns adversarial manipulation, data poisoning, model extraction, or prompt
injection, this document supplies precise, citable terms rather than NASA's more general security
language (our reading). It is a threat taxonomy for machine learning and generative AI (evasion, poisoning, prompt
injection and similar attacks).

**Key content for artificial intelligence / machine-learning assurance.**
- Predictive AI Taxonomy (Sec. 2, p.4): Evasion Attacks (Sec. 2.2, p.11), Poisoning Attacks (Sec. 2.3,
  p.19, including Backdoor Poisoning Sec. 2.3.3 and Model Poisoning Sec. 2.3.4), Privacy Attacks
  (Sec. 2.4, p.28, including Data Reconstruction, Membership Inference, Property Inference, Model
  Extraction), each with a named Mitigations subsection.
- Generative AI Taxonomy (Sec. 3, p.34): Supply Chain Attacks (Sec. 3.2, p.41), Direct Prompting
  Attacks (Sec. 3.3, p.43), Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks (Sec. 3.4, p.50), and Security of Agents
  (Sec. 3.5, p.54) — the agent-security subsection is directly relevant to agentic-AI risk candidates.
- Defines prompt injection: "A PROMPT INJECTION overrides these [system prompt] instructions,
  exploiting the concatenation of untrusted user output to the system prompt to induce unintended
  behavior" (Sec. 3.1.1, "GenAI Stages of Learning," p.36 ff. per TOC), and distinguishes Direct Prompt Injection from Indirect Prompt
  Injection (where a third party, not the user, supplies the injected content, Sec. 3.4, p.50).
- Artificial intelligence / machine learning touchpoint: the entire document is an adversarial
  machine-learning taxonomy; "machine learning," "algorithm," "adversarial," and "neural" occur
  throughout — no isolated bullet needed.

**Nearest NASA counterpart.** Compares to `NASA-HDBK-2203` and `NPR_7150.2D` — NASA's software
assurance documents address security and verification in general terms but do not name adversarial-ML
attack classes (evasion, poisoning, prompt injection) at this level of specificity (our reading).
